messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 51, Minh Tran described the disaster as the moment the world became something that could turn without warning. He had been visiting relatives in a coastal area during a severe storm season when the flooding came fast and chaotically. What stayed with him was not a single dramatic image so much as the sequence of unstable, bewildering moments: the power cutting out, the air turning thick with a scorched smell from damaged wiring and small fires breaking out nearby, neighbors shouting conflicting instructions, water rising where the ground had seemed safe only minutes earlier. He remembered trying to decide where to move his family and realizing that every choice suddenly felt uncertain. In the dark and confusion, with smoke mixing into the wet air, he had the sickening sense that his own judgment could not be trusted. Even now, when he spoke about it, he returned to that feeling of being overtaken by events he could not predict and by his own inability to feel sure of what to do next.

In the months after returning home to the United States, Minh expected the intensity of the experience to fade. Instead, he found himself reacting sharply to moments that seemed, even to him, strangely specific. If he woke with a headache, nausea, or the heavy body aches of an ordinary cold, he felt a jolt of alarm that was out of proportion to the illness itself. Feeling physically unwell seemed to transport him back to the disaster, when bodily discomfort had been tangled with fear, confusion, and danger. On those days he became preoccupied with the sense that something was about to go wrong. He watched himself closely and worried about how strongly he was reacting. At times he wondered whether these reactions meant he was going crazy. He was embarrassed by the thought, but it frightened him enough that he kept much of it to himself.

The smell of smoke was especially difficult. A faint odor from a backyard fire pit, burned food in the office microwave, or the acrid trace of overheated brakes in a parking garage could stop him in place. His body tensed before he could think. He would scan the room, the street, the air vents, trying to locate the source and judge whether there was immediate danger. Because the disaster had unfolded amid electrical burning and the possibility of fire in flooded buildings, smoke no longer seemed like a neutral smell to him. It meant conditions were shifting again, that safety might already be disappearing while other people remained unaware.

Unpredictability in general became hard for him to tolerate. Minh had built his adult life around careful planning, and as a policy analyst he was accustomed to order, contingencies, and clear lines of reasoning. Before the disaster, this had been one of his strengths. Afterward, situations that were loosely organized or liable to sudden change felt menacing. When meetings at work were rescheduled at the last minute, when a supervisor introduced an unplanned agenda item, or when transit delays threatened his commute, he felt his chest tighten and his mind race ahead to everything that could unravel. He had come to believe that he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. In the office, this meant he spent increasing amounts of time double-checking logistics, monitoring weather alerts, noticing unusual smells, and mapping exits in conference rooms before he could focus on the substance of a discussion.

These habits slowly changed his life. Colleagues noticed that Minh, once steady and thoughtful under pressure, had become rigid about schedules and visibly unsettled by unexpected changes. At home, his wife saw that ordinary disruptions—a child in the family getting sick, a power flicker during a storm, a last-minute change to dinner plans—could leave him withdrawn and keyed up for hours. Minh interpreted these reactions harshly. He was certain that if he were stronger, more dependable, he would be able to take things in stride. Instead, each episode seemed to confirm his private fear that he could not rely on himself anymore.

By the time he sought help, Minh was exhausted by the effort of staying ahead of things that might happen. He had recently left a work meeting after catching the smell of smoke from somewhere in the building and finding that he could no longer follow the conversation because he was too busy tracking possible danger. What finally pushed him toward treatment was less the single incident than what it seemed to say about his life now: that ordinary unpredictability, illness, and passing smells were narrowing his world. He came in frightened by the possibility that his reactions meant he was losing his mind, but also hoping, carefully, that there might be a way to feel steady again without having to stay on guard every moment.
